gates.title: Grade 9 motion rates, graphs, constant acceleration and circular speed

canonical_concepts.statement: Average rates are formed from total path or displacement over the same total elapsed time, not by blindly averaging listed speeds.
The familiar kinematic equations are exact only on an interval where acceleration is constant.
On a position-time graph, interval slope gives average velocity; on a velocity-time graph, interval slope gives average acceleration.
Uniform circular motion has constant speed v = 2 pi r / T while its velocity direction changes continuously.

relations.meaning: Average speed is total distance travelled divided by the positive elapsed time.
conditions: Delta t > 0.
distance_total >= 0.

relations.meaning: Average velocity is signed displacement divided by the same positive elapsed time.

symbols.meaning: Average velocity along the declared axis

conditions: Delta t > 0.
Delta x uses one declared axis/sign convention.

relations.meaning: For constant acceleration over the interval, final velocity equals initial velocity plus acceleration times elapsed time.

symbols.meaning: Final velocity along the declared axis
Initial velocity along the declared axis
Constant acceleration along the declared axis

conditions: Acceleration is constant over the whole interval.
u, v and a use one declared one-dimensional sign convention.

relations.meaning: For constant acceleration, signed displacement equals initial-velocity contribution plus the acceleration contribution over the interval.

symbols.meaning: Initial velocity along the declared axis
Constant acceleration along the declared axis

conditions: Acceleration is constant over the whole interval.
s, u and a use one declared one-dimensional sign convention.

relations.meaning: For constant acceleration, the squared velocities and signed displacement satisfy the no-time kinematic relation.

symbols.meaning: Final velocity along the declared axis
Initial velocity along the declared axis
Constant acceleration along the declared axis

conditions: Acceleration is constant over the whole interval.
u, v, a and s use one declared one-dimensional sign convention.

relations.meaning: Average acceleration over an interval is signed velocity change divided by the positive elapsed time.

symbols.meaning: Average acceleration along the declared axis

conditions: Delta t > 0.
Velocity values use one declared one-dimensional sign convention.

relations.meaning: For one complete uniform circular revolution, speed equals circumference divided by the positive period.

symbols.meaning: Constant speed around the circular path

conditions: Motion is uniform and the path is circular over the measured revolution.

relations.meaning: For constant acceleration, signed displacement over the interval is the signed geometric area under the straight velocity-time segment.

symbols.meaning: Initial velocity along the declared axis
Final velocity along the declared axis

conditions: Acceleration is constant over the whole interval, so the velocity-time segment is straight.
u, v and s use one declared one-dimensional sign convention.

validity_conditions: One finite interval with a positive elapsed time.
Average velocity requires a declared signed displacement convention.
Constant-acceleration relations are used only on intervals where one acceleration value describes the whole interval.
Graph-slope relations use two coordinates from the same graph and one declared axis convention.
Uniform circular speed uses one complete circular path of radius r completed in positive period T.
The graphical derivation treats displacement as signed velocity-time area over one constant-acceleration interval.

reasoning_sequence.action: Form the total path length and signed displacement over the same interval.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: Both averages must refer to the same elapsed interval.

reasoning_sequence.action: Divide each total by the common positive elapsed time.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: Rate over an interval is total change measure divided by elapsed time.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Average speed is always the arithmetic mean of the listed speeds.
misconceptions.counterexample: Equal-distance legs at unequal speeds spend unequal times at the two speeds.
misconceptions.repair: Use total distance divided by total time unless equal time weighting is explicitly given.

problem_families.title: Two-leg trips with path and displacement kept separate
hidden_invariants: Returning to the start can give nonzero average speed and zero average velocity.

falsification_cases.mutation: Replace the first relation's implemented validator reference with an undeclared validator id.

gates.title: Average and instantaneous mechanical power

canonical_concepts.statement: Power is a rate of energy transfer; an interval average and an instantaneous rate answer different questions.

relations.meaning: Average power is work transferred over a positive elapsed interval.

symbols.meaning: Net work transferred over the interval

conditions: Delta t > 0.
W is the net work assigned to the chosen system over that same interval.

relations.meaning: Instantaneous mechanical power is the signed force component along velocity times instantaneous speed.

symbols.meaning: Signed component of force along the instantaneous velocity direction

conditions: F_parallel carries the sign of the force component along or opposite the velocity direction.

validity_conditions: Average power uses one positive interval.
Instantaneous power uses quantities evaluated at the same instant.

reasoning_sequence.action: Decide whether the request is an interval average or an instantaneous rate.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: The two relations use different information.

reasoning_sequence.action: Evaluate the matching relation with a consistent work or force-velocity sign.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: Sign distinguishes transfer into versus out of the mechanical account.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Objects that receive the same work must have the same power.
misconceptions.counterexample: The same work delivered in half the time has twice the average power.
misconceptions.repair: Keep total transfer and transfer rate as separate quantities.

problem_families.title: Compare equal work delivered over unequal times or changing instantaneous rates
hidden_invariants: Equal total work does not imply equal power.

falsification_cases.mutation: Replace the first relation's implemented validator reference with an undeclared validator id.

gates.title: Newton's second law for net force and acceleration

canonical_concepts.statement: For a fixed positive mass, net force and acceleration are directed together and linked by F_net = m a.

relations.meaning: The vector net external force on a body equals its mass times its acceleration.

symbols.meaning: Net external force along the declared one-dimensional axis
Acceleration along the same declared axis

conditions: F_net and a refer to the same chosen body.
All signed components use one declared axis.

validity_conditions: Choose the body before summing external forces.
Use one inertial frame for the Grade 9 relation.
Mass is positive and treated as constant over the interval.

reasoning_sequence.action: Choose one body and one signed axis, then sum only external forces acting on that body.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: Newton's second law applies to the net external force on one chosen body.

reasoning_sequence.action: Set the signed net force equal to mass times signed acceleration.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Acceleration points in the direction of the largest individual force rather than the net force.
misconceptions.counterexample: Equal opposite forces can both be large while net force and acceleration are zero.
misconceptions.repair: Sum signed external forces first, then use the direction of F_net.

problem_families.title: One-dimensional net-force and acceleration problems
hidden_invariants: The same chosen body and sign convention are used in the force sum and acceleration.

falsification_cases.mutation: Replace the relation's validator reference with an undeclared id.

gates.title: Grade 9 work, kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy

canonical_concepts.statement: Constant-force work depends on the force component along displacement.
Kinetic energy depends on speed and gravitational potential energy near Earth depends on height relative to a declared reference.
Mechanical energy is conserved only when no additional transfer crosses the chosen mechanical account.
The Grade 9 kinetic- and raised-body potential-energy expressions are consequences of the work ledger plus already-authored force/motion relations, not isolated formulas.

relations.meaning: For a constant force component along a straight displacement, work equals the signed along-path force component times displacement.
conditions: Force component is constant over the displacement.
F_parallel uses the displacement direction as positive.

relations.meaning: Translational kinetic energy of a body in the declared reference frame.
conditions: One declared reference frame is used.

relations.expression: Delta U_g = m g Delta h
relations.meaning: Near Earth's surface with approximately uniform g, gravitational potential-energy change equals mass times g times vertical height change.
conditions: g is approximately uniform over the height change.
One height reference and positive-up convention are used.

relations.meaning: Net work on a body equals its change in translational kinetic energy.

symbols.meaning: Final kinetic energy minus initial kinetic energy

conditions: The same body and reference frame are used for the force work and kinetic energies.

relations.meaning: The chosen mechanical-energy account remains constant when no additional transfer crosses it.

symbols.meaning: Initial potential energy in the chosen interaction model

conditions: No frictional or outside transfer changes the chosen mechanical-energy account.
Initial and final energies use the same potential-energy reference.

relations.meaning: Near Earth's surface in an approximately uniform gravitational field, the weight-force magnitude on mass m is m times gravitational acceleration magnitude g.
conditions: Near-Earth field is treated as approximately uniform over the height range.
This relation gives the force magnitude; downward direction is supplied by the physical geometry.

validity_conditions: Choose the system/account before applying conservation.
Use the same reference frame and height reference consistently.
The Grade 9 derivation of K = 0.5 m v^2 uses a constant net force collinear with the displacement, so the constant-acceleration no-time relation applies.
The Grade 9 derivation of Delta U_g = m g Delta h uses a near-Earth approximately uniform g and a controlled lift whose applied force balances the weight.

reasoning_sequence.action: Choose the body/system, displacement direction and energy reference before selecting a relation.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: Work sign and energy values depend on those declarations.

reasoning_sequence.action: Choose work, kinetic energy, potential-energy change, work-energy, or conservation according to the stated transfer and account.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: Each relation answers a different bookkeeping question.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Any nonzero force on a moving body does positive work.
misconceptions.counterexample: A force perpendicular to displacement has zero along-path component and does zero work.
misconceptions.repair: Resolve force along displacement before multiplying.

problem_families.title: Grade 9 work and mechanical-energy ledgers
hidden_invariants: One system/account and one reference convention are used throughout.

falsification_cases.mutation: Replace the first relation's validator reference with an undeclared id.
